source_text: Ergo, inquitis, cur querimini quod vos insequamur, si pati vultis, cum diligere debeatis per quos patimini quod vultis? Plane volumus pati, verum eo more, quo et bellum nemo quidem libens patitur, cum et trepidare et periclitari sit necesse; tamen et proeliatur omnibus viribus, et vincens in proelio gaudet, qui de proelio querebatur, quia et gloriam consequitur et praedam. Proelium est nobis, quod provocamur ad tribunalia, ut illic sub discrimine capitis pro veritate certemus. Victoria est autem, pro quo certaveris, obtinere. Ea victoria habet, et gloriam placendi Deo, et praedam vivendi in aeternum. Sed obducimur, certe cum obtinuimus: ergo vicimus, cum occidimur; denique evadimus, cum obducimur: licet nunc sarmenticios et semaxios appelletis, quia ad stipitem dimidii axis revincti sarmentorum ambitu exurimur. Hic est habitus victoriae nostrae; haec palmata vestis; tali curru triumphamus. Merito itaque victis non placemus; propterea enim desperati et perditi existimamur. Sed haec desperatio et perditio penes vos, in caussa gloriae et famae, vexillum virtutis extollunt. Mucius dextram suam libens in ara reliquit: o sublimitas animi! Empedocles totum sese Catanensium Aetnaeis incendiis donavit: o vigor mentis! Aliqua Carthaginis conditrix rogo secundum matrimonium dedit: o praeconium castitatis! Regulus, ne unus pro multis hostibus viveret, toto corpore cruces patitur: o virum fortem et in captivitate victorem! Anaxarchus, cum in exemplum ptisanae pilo contunderetur: Tunde, tunde, aiebat, Anaxarchi follem, Anaxarchum enim non tundis: o philosophi magnanimitatem, qui de tali suo exitu etiam jocabatur! Omitto eos qui cum gladio proprio aliove genere mortis mitiore de laude pepigerunt. Ecce enim et tormentorum certamina coronantur a vobis. Attica meretrix, carnifice jam fatigato, postremo linguam suam comestam in faciem tyranni saevientis exspuit, ut exspueret et vocem, ne conjuratos confiteri posset, si etiam victa voluisset. Zeno Eleates, consultus a Dionysio quidnam philosophia praestaret, quum respondisset, contemptum mortis, flagellis tyranni subjectus sententiam suam ad mortem usque signabat. Certe Laconum flagella, sub oculis etiam hortantium propinquorum acerbata, tantum honorem tolerantiae domui conferunt, quantum sanguinis fuderint. O gloriam licitam, quia humanam, cui nec praesumptio perdita, nec persuasio desperata deputatur in contemptu mortis et atrocitatis omnimodae, cui tantum pro patria, pro agro, pro imperio, pro amicitia pati permissum est, quantum pro Deo non licet! Et tamen illis omnibus et statuas defunditis, et imagines inscribitis, et titulos inciditis in aeternitatem; quantum de monumentis potestis scilicet, praestatis et ipsi quodammodo mortuis resurrectionem. Hanc qui veram a Deo sperat, si pro Deo patiatur, insanus est. Sed hoc agite, boni Praesides, meliores multo apud populum, si illis Christianos immolaveritis. Cruciate, torquete, damnate, atterite nos: probatio est enim innocentiae nostrae iniquitas vestra. Ideo nos haec pati Deus patitur. Nam et proxime, ad lenonem damnando christianam potius quam ad leonem, confessi estis labem pudicitiae apud nos atrociorem omni poena et omni morte reputari. Nec quicquam tamen proficit exquisitior quaeque crudelitas vestra: illecebra est magis sectae. Plures efficimur, quoties metimur a vobis: semen est sanguis Christianorum. Multi apud vos ad tolerantiam doloris et mortis hortantur, ut Cicero in Tusculanis, ut Seneca in Fortuitis, ut Diogenes, ut Pyrrhon, ut Callinicus. Nec tamen tantos inveniunt verba discipulos, quantos Christiani factis docendo. Illa ipsa obstinatio, quam exprobratis, magistra est. Quis enim non contemplatione ejus concutitur ad requirendum, quid intus in re sit? Quis non, ubi requisivit, accedit, ubi accessit, pati exoptat, ut totam Dei gratiam redimat, ut omnem veniam ab eo compensatione sanguinis sui expediat? Omnia enim huic operi delicta donantur. Inde est, quod ibidem sententiis vestris gratias agimus; ut est aemulatio divinae rei et humanae, cum damnamur a vobis, a Deo absolvimur.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, you say, why do we complain that you persecute us, if we are willing to suffer, since we ought to love those through whom we suffer what we want? Certainly we want to suffer, but in the way that no one willingly endures war, although it is necessary to tremble and be in danger; nevertheless, one fights with all his strength, and the one who conquers in battle rejoices, who complained about the battle, because he also achieves glory and booty. The battle for us is what we are provoked to, the tribunals, so that there we may contend for the truth under danger of death. Victory, however, is to obtain what you have contended for. This victory has both the glory of pleasing God and the booty of living eternally. But we are covered, certainly when we obtain it: therefore we conquer when we are killed; finally, we escape when we are covered: although now you call us worthless and deserving of death, because we are burned, bound to a stake, surrounded by a bundle of sticks. This is the appearance of our victory; this is the robe of triumph; in such a chariot we triumph. Therefore, we do not please the defeated; for we are considered desperate and lost. But this desperation and loss, in the cause of glory and fame, raise the banner of virtue. Mucius willingly left his right hand on the altar: oh, the loftiness of his soul! Empedocles gave his whole self to the fires of Aetna: oh, the strength of his mind! Some founder of Carthage gave herself to the pyre as a second marriage: oh, the praise of chastity! Regulus, so that one man would not live for many enemies, endures crosses on his whole body: oh, strong man and conqueror in captivity! Anaxarchus, when he was being pounded like a pestle, said, 'Pound, pound the shell of Anaxarchus, for you are not pounding Anaxarchus': oh, the magnanimity of the philosopher, who even joked about his own death! I pass over those who have made a bargain about praise with their own sword or some other kind of milder death. For, behold, even the contests of torments are crowned by you. The Attic courtesan, when the executioner was already tired, finally spat her chewed-up tongue into the face of the raging tyrant, so that she might also spit out her voice, lest she be able to confess the conspirators, even if she had wanted to, when defeated. Zeno of Elea, when consulted by Dionysius what philosophy offered, when he responded, 'contempt of death', was subjected to the tyrant's whips, and he sealed his sentence to death. Certainly, the whips of the Laconians, made more bitter under the eyes of even encouraging relatives, bring as much honor of endurance to the house as they have shed blood. Oh, the glory that is permitted, because it is human, to which neither lost presumption nor desperate persuasion is ascribed in contempt of death and every kind of cruelty, for which it is permitted to suffer as much for country, for field, for empire, for friendship, as it is not permitted for God! And yet, you pour out statues and inscribe images and engrave titles for all these people into eternity; as much as you are able from monuments, you also provide a kind of resurrection for the dead. He who hopes for true resurrection from God, if he suffers for God, is insane. But do this, good Presidents, you will be more pleasing to the people if you sacrifice Christians to them. Crucify, torture, condemn, destroy us: for your injustice is the proof of our innocence. For this reason, God allows us to suffer these things. For recently, by condemning a Christian to a pimp rather than to a lion, you confessed that the stain of impurity is considered more severe among us than any punishment or death. Nor does your cruelty, no matter how refined, accomplish anything: it is rather an enticement to the sect. We become more numerous, whenever we are measured by you: the blood of Christians is seed. Many among you encourage endurance of pain and death, like Cicero in the Tusculans, like Seneca in the Fortuitous, like Diogenes, like Pyrrho, like Callinicus. And yet, they do not find as many disciples with words as Christians do by teaching with deeds. That very obstinacy, which you reproach, is a teacher. For who is not moved by contemplating it to seek what is inside the matter? Who, when he has sought, does not approach, and when he has approached, does not desire to suffer, so that he may redeem the whole grace of God, so that he may obtain all forgiveness from him in exchange for his own blood? For all sins are forgiven in this work. Hence, it is that we give thanks for your sentences; as there is an emulation of divine and human things, when we are condemned by you, we are absolved by God.

choices.why: metaphorical extension of war to spiritual struggle
ironic use of military term for Christian martyrdom

pass_b_english: So you ask why we complain that you persecute us, if we are willing to suffer, since we ought to love those through whom we suffer what we want. We certainly want to suffer, but only the way no one willingly endures war, even though it is necessary to tremble and face danger; still, one fights with all his strength, and the victor rejoices in battle even though he complained of it, because he also gains glory and plunder. Our war is what we are provoked into — the courts — so that there we may contend for the truth under danger of death. Victory, however, is obtaining what you have contended for. This victory carries both the glory of pleasing God and the prize of living forever. But we are overwhelmed precisely when we have secured it: therefore we conquer when we are killed; finally we escape when we are overwhelmed — even though you now call us worthless kindling and half-axle victims, because we are burned, bound to a stake, encircled by a bundle of sticks. This is the look of our victory; this is the triumphal robe; in such a chariot we triumph. No wonder, then, that we do not please the defeated; that is why we are considered desperate and lost. But this desperation and loss, in the cause of glory and fame, raise the banner of virtue. Mucius willingly left his right hand on the altar: oh, the loftiness of his soul! Empedocles gave his whole self to the fires of Aetna: oh, the strength of his mind! Some founder of Carthage gave herself to the pyre as a second marriage: oh, the praise of chastity! Regulus, so that one man would not live for many enemies, endures crosses on his whole body: oh, the strong man and conqueror in captivity! Anaxarchus, when he was being pounded like a pestle, said, 'Pound, pound the shell of Anaxarchus, for you are not pounding Anaxarchus': oh, the magnanimity of the philosopher, who even joked about his own death! I pass over those who made a bargain for praise with their own sword or some other milder death. For look: even the contests of torments are crowned by you. The Attic courtesan, when the executioner was already tired, finally spat her chewed-up tongue into the face of the raging tyrant, so that she might also spit out her voice, lest she be able to confess the conspirators, even if she had wanted to, when defeated. Zeno of Elea, when consulted by Dionysius what philosophy offered, answered 'contempt of death,' and was subjected to the tyrant's whips, sealing his sentence to death. Certainly, the whips of the Laconians, made more bitter under the eyes of even encouraging relatives, bring as much honor of endurance to the house as they have shed blood. Oh, the glory that is permitted because it is human — to which neither lost presumption nor desperate persuasion is ascribed in contempt of death and every kind of cruelty, for which it is permitted to suffer as much for country, for field, for empire, for friendship as it is not permitted for God! And yet you pour out statues, inscribe images, and engrave titles for all these people into eternity; as far as monuments can do it, you yourselves provide a kind of resurrection for the dead. Anyone who hopes for true resurrection from God, if he suffers for God, is insane. But do this, good Presidents — you will be far more pleasing to the people if you sacrifice Christians to them. Crucify, torture, condemn, destroy us: your injustice is the proof of our innocence. For this reason God allows us to suffer these things. For recently, by condemning a Christian woman to a pimp rather than to a lion, you confessed that the stain of impurity is considered more severe among us than any punishment or death. Nor does your cruelty, no matter how refined, accomplish anything: it is rather an enticement to the sect. We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you: the blood of Christians is seed. Many among you encourage endurance of pain and death — like Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations, like Seneca in On Providence, like Diogenes, like Pyrrho, like Callinicus. Yet they do not find as many disciples with words as Christians do by teaching with deeds. That very obstinacy you reproach is a teacher. For who is not shaken by contemplating it into seeking what lies inside the matter? Who, having sought, does not draw near, and having drawn near, does not desire to suffer, so that he may redeem the whole grace of God, so that he may obtain all forgiveness from Him in exchange for his own blood? For all sins are forgiven in this work. Hence we give thanks for your sentences; it is an emulation of the divine and the human: when we are condemned by you, we are absolved by God.
